item.title: Diddy & Dudus Fight Claim Shot Down By Federal Prison Officials
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Federal prison officials rejected the Diddy-Dudus fight claim while declining to explain the cause of his reported head injury.
item.content:encoded:
Federal prison officials flatly denied Diddy’s alleged fight with Christopher “Dudus” Coke on Thursday.

The Bureau of Prisons rejected the claim that the two men clashed at FCI Fort Dix in New Jersey. A spokesperson told TMZ, “We can tell you that the story you are referring to is false and did not happen.”

Prison officials did not say what caused the reported injury. When asked how Diddy was hurt, the bureau declined to share more details.

The outlet stood by its account of a medical trip. It said Diddy left Fort Dix by ambulance early Saturday, October 10, for treatment of a head injury and returned before dawn. The report described the injury as non-life-threatening.

The agency’s denial followed the outlet’s report that Dudus fought with Diddy a day before that trip. That account linked the alleged clash to anger over raids and seized phones at the prison, citing sources inside Fort Dix.

Officials had given a more guarded response when news of the reported injury first broke.

Fort Dix told Us Weekly on October 12 that it would not discuss any prisoner’s housing or medical status. It cited privacy, safety and security.

Diddy’s team told the magazine it was still trying to confirm what happened. His representative said, “Sean’s health and well-being are our immediate concern.”

The official response came after sources close to Dudus had also denied the fight.

Nationwide Radio Jamaica said its newsroom spoke with those sources Wednesday evening. They said Dudus had never crossed paths with Diddy at Fort Dix. The station said their account led it to amend its first report.

Dudus’ aunt, Angela Jackson, had also rejected the claim. Nationwide cited her Instagram statement saying the men had never met and were held in different sections of the prison. The broadcaster did not name the separate sources it interviewed.

Diddy was serving a 50-month term after his federal trial. Jurors convicted him of two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution and acquitted him of racketeering conspiracy and sex trafficking.

His legal team appealed his conviction and sentence. In an October 7 statement to Us Weekly, his spokesperson said, “Sean remains focused on serving his time.”

item.title: Adrien Broner & DeenTheGreat Turn Kai Cenat Feud Into Diss Track
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Adrien Broner and DeenTheGreat targeted Kai Cenat in “Purple App Killa,” while Lemuel Plummer offered a different view of the feud.
item.content:encoded:
Former four-division boxing champion Adrien Broner and DeenTheGreat took their feud with Kai Cenat into the studio and released “Purple App Killa,” a new diss track and music video with Hitmaka.

DeenTheGreat named Kai Cenat as the target when he announced the October 15 release. “KAI CENAT DISS TRACK OUT NOW,” he wrote in a post on X, directing fans to the full video.

The pair had already shared behind-the-scenes footage of work on the song and its music video before the finished clip went live. Broner and DeenTheGreat both appeared as collaborators on the official upload, which ran just under three minutes.

The release followed DeenTheGreat’s public complaint about visiting Kai’s Vivet clothing stand at ComplexCon. He said he came to support the brand and spend money but felt like a random fan.

Their complaints circulated on October 5, more than a week before DeenTheGreat announced the finished track.

He and Ray J discussed the dispute with Zeus Network founder Lemuel Plummer, who had a different account of his own visit to the stand.

NDTV Sports reported that Plummer bought six outfits from Vivet. During the exchange, DeenTheGreat argued that Kai should have given Plummer clothes for free.

Plummer said he had chosen to pay because he wanted to support the business. He also said Kai had thanked him for coming through.

“I bought it. I wanted to support it,” Plummer said.

DeenTheGreat kept pressing the point about the clothes. Plummer instead credited Kai with building the brand with his own money and described a warm reception at the booth.

He offered to call Kai during the discussion. DeenTheGreat told him not to bother. Plummer held to his own account: “Well, he did give me respect.”

As the diss video arrived, DeenTheGreat also had a live event with Hitmaka and KICK. The platform billed the producer as the DJ for its COB Halloween Bash, a Miami party presented by KICK and DeenTheGreat.

The event was billed as KICK-exclusive. DeenTheGreat posted that the bash was live shortly after he announced the song.

item.title: Marsha Blackburn’s Kendrick Lamar AI Ad Triggers ELVIS Act Warning
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Marsha Blackburn called her Kendrick Lamar AI clip a “funsie” as a Nashville attorney questioned whether its use had clearance.
item.content:encoded:
Marsha Blackburn’s AI take on Kendrick Lamar’s Super Bowl show drew a legal warning from a Nashville attorney, who said the campaign post could run afoul of Tennessee’s ELVIS Act if the rapper hadn’t approved its use.

Entertainment lawyer Kaley Bonett told WKRN that she viewed the clip as a campaign ad. She pointed to Kendrick Lamar’s voice and his halftime choreography to explain why clearance mattered.

Bonett is an associate at Hall Booth Smith, where she works on entertainment and intellectual property matters.

Blackburn said a county commissioner made the video, and she and other Republicans reposted it.

“We re-posted it, and it’s a funsie. Everybody got out and vote,” she said.

The senator posted the clip October 13 to promote early voting in her run for Tennessee governor. It cast her in Kendrick Lamar’s Super Bowl role, with AI versions of other Tennessee Republicans joining the performance. Democratic rival Jerri Green criticized the post.

The earlier backlash also highlighted Blackburn’s push to protect artists from AI copies of their voices and faces.

On September 30, Blackburn asked the Senate to pass the NO FAKES Act without objection. She argued that artists, songwriters and other Americans needed protection from harmful deepfakes made without their consent.

The bill would create federal rights over AI replicas of a person’s voice and face, with a process to seek their removal from online platforms. Sen. Ted Cruz blocked that attempt, saying the measure needed stronger free-speech protections.

Blackburn pushed back. She said the bill already included language to protect political commentary, criticism, satire and parody. That exchange showed how permission and free speech had become central to her own case for federal action.

Tennessee’s ELVIS Act took effect July 1, 2024. It added voice protections to state law, covering both real and simulated voices that people can identify. It allows claims for certain uses made without consent and lets courts order them to stop.

The state law also allows news, public affairs, criticism, satire and parody when the First Amendment protects those uses. Those speech protections sit alongside the voice rights Bonett raised in her assessment.

Before its October 15 update, the station reported no response to its requests for further comment from Blackburn or Kendrick Lamar’s team.

item.title: Diddy Moved To Allenwood Prison After Brawl With Jamaican Drug Lord
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Diddy changed prisons amid scrutiny of his conduct behind bars, disputed fight claims and a 50-month federal sentence.
item.content:encoded:
Diddy moved from Fort Dix to Allenwood Friday, federal officials told TMZ. No reason was disclosed.

FCI Allenwood Low, in Pennsylvania, has the same low-security classification as Fort Dix. Diddy’s lawyers had sought the New Jersey placement so he could enter a drug treatment program that offered a chance to shorten his time behind bars.

Diddy, whose legal name is Sean Combs, arrived at Fort Dix from Brooklyn’s Metropolitan Detention Center on October 30, 2025. ABC News reported then that he was housed in the treatment program’s unit rather than the general population.

The move followed his 50-month sentence for two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution. Jurors acquitted him of sex trafficking and racketeering conspiracy.

Successful completion of the Residential Drug Abuse Program can bring eligible inmates up to a year off their sentences.

The Bureau of Prisons ties that benefit to completing treatment and meeting its other requirements.

His stay in New Jersey drew fresh attention last month when NBC News investigated claims that he received special treatment.

Former fellow inmates alleged he had access to banned electronics and liquor and paid other prisoners to cook, clean and provide massages. His team maintained he was following prison rules.

NBC later reported that officials sanctioned Diddy for disruptive conduct and took away 41 days of good-conduct time, citing a union official.

The punishment followed its investigation into his alleged prison perks.

Union official Jose Rojas separately told TMZ that Diddy’s disciplinary history listed July 31 and September 30 fights and phone violations.

More recently, accounts of a fight with fellow prisoner Christopher “Dudus” Coke prompted a direct denial from federal officials.

The Bureau of Prisons told USA TODAY on October 15 that the reported incident did not happen.

Diddy’s representative, Juda Engelmayer, also told the outlet that his team had no verified information showing he had been attacked or injured.

The agency’s public inmate locator still listed Fort Dix when AllHipHop checked Friday morning. It showed a projected release date of March 2, 2028.

The locator cautions that release dates can change as the agency reviews sentences and recalculates credits under the First Step Act.

item.title: Digital Underground’s Money B Reveals The Truth About Tupac, Shock G’s Humpty Hump Struggles & Untold History
item.dc:creator: Chuck Creekmur (@ChuckCreekmur)
item.description: Digital Underground's Money B reveals how Tupac really joined the group, and why Shock G grew frustrated with Humpty Hump's fame.
item.content:encoded:
Money B Tells His Story…

Before Tupac Shakur became one of Hip-Hop’s most influential figures, before “The Humpty Dance” turned Digital Underground into a household name, and before Shock G’s alter ego Humpty Hump became larger than life, there was a collective of young artists in Oakland determined to do something different.

Money B was there for nearly all of it.

Born in Philadelphia and raised in the Bay Area, the veteran MC grew up surrounded by revolutionary politics. Both of his parents were members of the Black Panther Party, and he attended Oakland Community School, where Huey P. Newton personally handed him his graduation certificate.

That foundation would eventually intersect with one of Hip-Hop’s most creative groups and one of its most iconic artists, Tupac Shakur.

Now, with his new book, A D.U. Party Don’t Stop: The Money B Story, Money B is revisiting the triumphs, tensions and unexpected moments that helped shape his extraordinary journey. (Click here to purchase this riveting memoir.)

In this candid conversation with AllHipHop’s Chuck “Jigsaw” Creekmur and DJ Thoro, Money B discusses everything from Tupac’s early days and their shared political upbringing to Shock G’s frustration with Humpty Hump’s popularity. He also addresses an unusual viral photograph of himself with Tupac and recalls the night Digital Underground deliberately got booed at the Apollo Theater.

The Interview

AllHipHop (Chuck Creekmur): Your parents were Black Panthers?

Money B: Yes. Both my mom and my dad joined the Black Panthers at the Philadelphia chapter in 1970, I want to say. Then my dad moved to the Bay like a year or two later. About a year after that, me and my mom followed.

Shortly after, that’s where I attended Oakland Community School.

AllHipHop: What was the difference between that school and a regular public school?

Money B: You were placed in class not by your age, but by your aptitude. However much you were able to learn, you weren’t held back.

Another thing about the school is we were taught how to learn as opposed to being forced what to learn. It was encouraged to ask questions, to be inquisitive.

I probably read Malcolm X when I was like 11. They would teach us about Marcus Garvey, and we knew about Langston Hughes. I actually met Rosa Parks. She came and visited.

AllHipHop: There’s a picture of you and Huey P. Newton in the book. What’s the story?

Money B: That’s when I graduated from Oakland Community School, basically sixth-grade age. Every year, Huey P. would usually be there at the graduation ceremony, and he’d be the one to hand out the diploma.

That’s a picture of Huey P. Newton giving me my certificate of graduation. That’s actually my brother and sister in the picture with me.

DJ Thoro: With that upbringing, was there any conflict when you wanted to get into the music business?

Money B: My father always hoped that I would talk more about pro-Black, socially conscious music because he loved Public Enemy and Paris.

He actually was a consultant on Paris’s video. When Paris came out, he reached out to my dad.

AllHipHop: What was the original concept of Digital Underground before the group became what we knew?

Money B: Originally, Shock wanted Digital Underground to be more like a pro-Black militant group.

But back then, you couldn’t be a biter. Up until Public Enemy came out, it was like, somebody’s doing it. We can’t do that. We couldn’t come out wearing dashikis because the Jungle Brothers were already doing that.

If you really pay close attention, Digital Underground’s music always has an underlying message. We just weren’t over the top with it.

We make you dance, want you to have fun, party, kick it with us, but also learn a little something along the way.

Shock’s main message, at least the way I interpreted it, was about unity and bringing everybody together.

AllHipHop: How did you and Shock G actually meet?

Money B: Digital Underground put a record out in 1988 called “Underwater Rimes.” At that time, it was just Shock and Chopmaster J.

They needed a DJ. DJ Fuze was recognized as probably one of the hottest DJs in the Bay, and me and Fuze were a group called Raw Fusion.

They came to the crib, and Fuze was renting a room in my mom’s apartment. So I’m there with these guys coming to take my DJ!

After the meeting, Fuze agreed to work with them, but only under the condition that they work with us. We’re a group. We’re not breaking up.

AllHipHop: Digital Underground eventually became a huge collective.

Money B: It definitely was a collective. Everybody came in with the understanding that the goal was for everybody to get their own deal and project.

We were literally Wu-Tang before Wu-Tang.

When Pac came aboard, he was a solo artist. Me and Fuze were Raw Fusion before we got in the group, knowing this was going to help us get a deal for a Raw Fusion album, a Tupac album, Saafir and everybody else.

AllHipHop: How did Tupac come into the group? Was he trying to get down with you guys?

Money B: No, that’s not how it happened.

He was a solo artist signed to TNT Records, which was the label we were signed to.

Before he was a solo artist, he was in a group called Strictly Dope with Ray Luv. They were working on their demo, so they were around us.

Pac and I were close to the same age. When he used to come to Oakland, my house was the hangout house. Me and Fuze had the equipment, turntables, records, and my block was active. Pac liked that.

It got to a point where I think Atron feared he might lose him because it was taking too long, in Tupac’s opinion, for him to get a deal.

We were about to go on our first U.S. tour, and Atron asked if we could bring him.

Everybody likes to say he was a dancer. His job description was just to come and help us with whatever we needed help with.

It could be dancing, helping break down equipment, all these things we all did. He wasn’t just a roadie. He would rhyme, sometimes be the hype man. We all had roles.

AllHipHop: Did you and Pac connect as Panther Cubs, since both your parents were Black Panthers?

Money B: Yes and no.

We didn’t sit around and have meetings about how we were going to take down the white man. We didn’t do that.

But because we had similar upbringings, when he would talk about what people thought were radical thoughts, his messaging was never foreign to me.

When he mentioned political prisoners, Geronimo Pratt and Assata Shakur, I knew who these people were.

He didn’t have to explain anything to me. I think there was probably some comfort in that.

It was unspoken.

AllHipHop: Let’s talk about Humpty Hump. Did he eventually become bigger than Digital Underground?

Money B: He became the star. There became a point where Humpty was bigger than the entire group.

More importantly, he was bigger than Shock G, but Shock G was the one who created him.

Shock openly admitted that some chicks would want him to put the nose on!

He told us the first time Humpty Hump really got busy. Shock G didn’t get it. Humpty got it!

But Shock was such a great musician, and he wanted to be recognized for that.

At one point, he felt like all people wanted was Humpty. He wasn’t trying to kill Humpty, but he wasn’t excited to keep doing it.

I think The Body-Hat Syndrome album was a way to go in the opposite direction because Tommy Boy wanted more Humpty pop songs.

He didn’t want to give them another Humpty hit because then he would be pigeonholed forever.

AllHipHop (DJ Thoro): I was at the Apollo when you guys came out with bags over your heads and everybody started booing. Who planned that?

Money B: We were at rehearsal, goofing around. I think Pee Wee came up with the idea because of the Unknown Comic from The Gong Show.

Shock was like, “No, let’s really do that.”

But the only way it would work was if we got booed. We had to think of the wackest everything to make sure we got booed.

We couldn’t let production know. The Sandman didn’t know. Kiki Shepard didn’t know. Mark Curry didn’t know.

Mark’s from Oakland, and I knew him. If I had said something, he would have recognized my voice.

When we revealed ourselves, they went crazy. New York love was crazy!

AllHipHop: There’s also that picture of you and Tupac that people keep talking about. Can you clarify it?

Money B: I get it. If I was a friend of that person in that situation, I’d be cracking on them.

But back then, if you were on the road, the only person who had their own room was the star, which was Shock.

Other than that, me and Pac were roommates. Fuze and Money? Everybody had a roommate.

Obviously, he sat down and took a picture. I don’t know what else you want me to say.

Other than that, you’re implying something, and if you know me, it’s ridiculous. If you don’t know me, that’s fine, too.

AllHipHop: Nothing to see here?

Money B: Nothing to see.

Editor’s note: The interview has been condensed and lightly edited for clarity. The final exchange refers to Money B and Tupac sharing a room while touring, with other group members also assigned roommates.

item.title: Cori Broadus Lands “Doggyland” Role & Helps Create New Character
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Cori Broadus voices Maxine in Snoop Dogg's "Doggyland," helping create the character after a childhood cartoon audition.
item.content:encoded:
Cori Broadus turned a childhood dream into a role she helped build, joining her father Snoop Dogg‘s animated children’s series “Doggyland” as the voice of Maxine.

The confident labradoodle marks Cori’s animation debut, The Hollywood Reporter revealed. Cori worked with co-creator Claude Brooks on the character’s look and personality, giving her more to do than just record.

As a child, Cori auditioned for “The Backyardigans” but did not get the part. Her long-held wish now has a new home in Maxine, who appears in the music video for “You’re Enough,” the title track from the show’s latest album.

The role builds on a project that Snoop launched in August 2022 with Brooks and singer-songwriter October London. Snoop voices Bow Wizzle, the grown-up dog who guides the puppies through their world.

From the start, the team built “Doggyland” around music that children and parents could enjoy together. Its dogs sing, dance and rap through lessons on letters, numbers, good habits and how to treat other people. The goal was to pair catchy songs with messages about kindness, confidence and accepting differences.

For Snoop, the idea grew out of his roles as a father, grandfather and youth football coach. At the show’s launch, he said he wanted to create a positive place for children that reflected the culture in both its music and characters. Making it available on YouTube and YouTube Kids also gave families free access.

The show’s early videos were usually under five minutes and paired familiar nursery rhymes with lessons on feelings, sharing and bullying. A Common Sense Media review noted that its sharing lesson goes beyond passing things around to include sharing emotions with others.

That mission has also moved beyond the screen. A partnership with Little Bee Books, announced late last year, set out to bring the songs into board books, sound books and activities. The first title adapted the show’s affirmations song, giving families another way to use its messages in daily life.

Maxine adds Cori’s own personality to that world. Snoop said he was proud to see his daughter become a cartoon character she had helped create.

“I love that she’s confident, a little sassy, and encourages kids to be themselves,” Cori said.

item.title: Chocolate MC Sued Over Alleged Assault Of Teen After Las Vegas Club Show
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Chocolate MC faces a Vegas civil suit over an alleged assault after a club show, with the nightclub and hotel owner also named.
item.content:encoded:
Chocolate MC is being sued over the alleged sexual assault of a teen after a Las Vegas club show. The club and hotel owner Boyd Gaming also faces claims.

The Las Vegas Review-Journal reported the plaintiff was 16 at the alleged assault. Her lawyers sued Chocolate MC, whose legal name is Yosvanis Sierra Hernandez, on October 13.

The complaint says Masque Nightclub let her obtain alcohol and cocaine on December 31, 2024. It alleges Chocolate MC gave her more drugs and alcohol before sexually assaulting her at The Orleans.

The suit faults Masque’s owners for underage drinking and Boyd for failing to protect her. It seeks more than $15,000 on each of 13 claims.

The Review-Journal found no related criminal charge. Boyd declined to comment, and the club’s registered agent did not reply. The report did not include a response from Chocolate MC.

The Nevada suit is separate from the Florida case that put Chocolate MC in prison, which grew from the 2024 killing of Cuban reggaeton star El Taiger.

Prosecutors accused Damian Valdez-Galloso of killing the singer and Chocolate MC of trying to have Valdez-Galloso killed in jail.

A Miami jury found Chocolate MC guilty of soliciting first-degree murder in November 2025, the Miami Herald reported from his one-day trial.

Prosecutors said he used social media and an interview to offer inmates $20,000 in commissary money, then raised the sum to $100,000. They argued the posts could solicit violence without a direct message to an inmate and cited a song used in one post as evidence of intent.

Chocolate MC took the stand to deny trying to get anyone killed and said his posts were meant to promote an album.

He told jurors he had known El Taiger for about 20 years. His lawyer described the statements as a joke made in grief, but the jury rejected that position.

His conviction left other Florida charges unsettled, including accusations of threatening and abducting a fan.

In March, Chocolate MC accepted a plea agreement covering the solicitation count and separate cases, Univision Miami reported from the hearing. The deal brought a 10-year prison sentence followed by five years of probation.

item.title: Summer Walker’s Label Battle Reaches Point Of No Return Amid Fraud Accusations
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Summer Walker accused LVRN of withholding merch and YouTube income as she sought damages and an end to her 2017 agreement.
item.content:encoded:
Summer Walker sued Love Renaissance for fraud and sought to end her label and management deal over money she claimed the company kept.

The case became public this week through reporting by Rolling Stone and Billboard. Summer Walker filed the suit August 28, weeks before Interscope brought its separate $50 million claim against her.

Summer Walker accused LVRN of taking funds set aside for her tours, music, marketing and merchandise. She claimed the firm used those budgets to cover excessive company costs.

The disputed income included Amazon sales of goods carrying her name and image. Summer Walker alleged that LVRN sold those items through Amazon and other sites but failed to pay her a share of the sales.

She also accused LVRN of running a YouTube account she hadn’t known about. She claimed the firm erased the account’s past data before putting her in charge and never paid her any income from it.

Her lawyer, Keith Moten, said on Tuesday that her main goal was to end the deal.

“Most importantly, we also have very strong legal grounds for the court to order Summer’s release from her deal with LVRN as well,” Moten told Rolling Stone.

Billboard reported that Summer Walker described a deal that gave LVRN control beyond her music. She said it covered touring, merchandise and use of her name and image. Summer Walker alleged that no independent lawyer advised her before she signed.

Her fight with LVRN began before Interscope sued her on October 9. She had told Interscope she would stop working under its deal as of August 27, citing California’s seven-year rule. Interscope sought damages over recordings it said she still owed under a five-album commitment, while Summer Walker disputed its claims.

LVRN had moved toward a wider independent business, but it kept ties to Interscope involving Summer Walker.

In a June interview, LVRN CEO Tunde Balogun said the companies still worked together on Summer Walker and 6lack. For its broader business, LVRN chose Sony-owned The Orchard to distribute its music.

The new allegations followed a different public account of her deal in 2021. Summer Walker pushed back on reports about her original contract at the time, saying her terms had changed and she had her own representation and LVRN’s support.

LVRN did not respond to either outlet’s request for comment before their Tuesday reports. Summer Walker sought damages as well as an order voiding her September 15, 2017, agreement with the company.

item.title: Chance The Rapper Wins Against Ex-Manager Again After $35 Victory
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Chance the Rapper won a new ruling against Pat Corcoran over merchandise profits after his earlier $35 jury victory.
item.content:encoded:
Chance the Rapper won another round against Pat Corcoran after a judge ordered his former manager to hand over undisclosed merchandise profits, months after the rapper won a courtroom battle that netted him just $35.

Cook County Circuit Court Judge James E. Hanlon Jr. ruled on October 13 that Corcoran breached his duties to Chance by seeking side payments from merchandise vendors without telling him. Rolling Stone, which obtained the ruling, reported that the repayment order covered vendor commissions and merchandise-related management fees.

The court ordered Corcoran to return those profits, along with the 15% management commissions he earned on merchandise during the period at issue. The court also directed him to hand over chanceraps.com, the domain used to sell the artist’s merchandise.

The amount still needs to be worked out. Chance’s representatives said they could recover as much as $1.5 million in management fees, plus vendor payments. The judge had not set a final dollar figure. A court conference in late November is set to address the calculation, Billboard reported.

“I’m grateful to finally close this chapter of my life and can’t wait to eventually tell my side of the story. I’m thankful to the courts and, more importantly, to God for remaining faithful,” Chance said in a statement supplied by his representatives.

The new decision covered a claim the judge heard in May, separate from the jury trial that ended in March.

That jury rejected Corcoran’s $3.8 million demand for unpaid commissions and awarded Chance $35 on his own counterclaims. The dispute over the manager’s duty to act in his client’s interests still had to be decided.

Corcoran sued in 2020 after Chance fired him that April. Their working relationship had begun in 2012, but they never signed a written management contract.

The former manager argued that their verbal deal entitled him to a share of income for three years after the split. Chance denied agreeing to those continued payments.

Their fight also reached beyond post-split income. Corcoran’s side argued that he should earn commissions on deals he worked on while employed, even though the money arrived later.

Chance’s lawyers accused him of pursuing his own profit through merchandise arrangements rather than protecting the artist’s business.

The judge rejected Chance’s request that Corcoran forfeit all past compensation, preserving payment for work outside the disputed merchandise arrangements.

Corcoran’s spokesperson emphasized that limit in a response to Rolling Stone and argued that Chance still had to prove harm in the merchandise business.

“The court ruled there is no basis for Chance’s claim of more than $10 million in damages,” the spokesperson said.

item.title: Drakeo The Ruler’s Estate Reaches Settlement In Live Nation Battle
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Drakeo The Ruler's family spent years fighting promoters over backstage security after his fatal 2021 festival stabbing.
item.content:encoded:
Drakeo The Ruler‘s estate reached a conditional settlement with Live Nation, TMZ reported. Financial details weren’t specified.

The family’s fight over backstage safety had stretched for years after the Los Angeles rapper was fatally stabbed at the Once Upon A Time in LA festival. He was 28 when he was attacked behind the main stage on December 18, 2021, and later died at a hospital.

On December 20, 2021, his mother, Darrylene Corniel, told Rolling Stone that venue security had failed her son.

“This happened backstage at an event. Someone has to be held accountable,” Corniel said.

She told the outlet that witnesses had described a large crowd overwhelming the small group that accompanied her sons. His brother, Ralfy The Plug, had tried to protect him, she said.

Corniel also described being unable to hug or kiss her son at the hospital. She had to see him through a window because his death was being treated as a homicide.

“I will not rest until justice is served,” she said in that interview.

Separate complaints followed from his mother, brother and son. In January 2023, Rolling Stone reported that Judge Yolanda Orozco allowed his brother and members of their Stinc Team collective to pursue claims against Live Nation and other defendants.

They alleged that vehicle searches were inadequate, guards were absent from the backstage VIP area, and nobody stopped the attack. Their claims included negligence, unsafe premises and emotional distress.

Live Nation argued that the attack was unforeseeable because no similar incident had occurred at the venue. Orozco ruled that the absence of a prior attack did not automatically bar their claims.

Judge James I. Montgomery had denied the estate’s request for financial records from Live Nation Worldwide and C3 Presents. Its lawyers argued that they had shown a strong likelihood of winning punitive damages, but Montgomery was not persuaded.

The promoters’ lawyers denied intentional wrongdoing. They said they hired a specialist to assess risks, plan security and coordinate vendors and law enforcement.
